articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities and Issues New Cuba FAQs
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities in Iran. This action is part of ongoing efforts to counter activities deemed detrimental to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In a separate but related development, OFAC also issued updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning Cuba. These FAQs aim to provide clarity and guidance to individuals and entities regarding U.S. sanctions policies related to Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Amends Russia-related GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. These actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting global criminal networks.

Concurrently, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License to facilitate certain humanitarian-related transactions. Furthermore, an amended Russia-related General License and associated Frequently Asked Questions were released, providing updated guidance on authorized activities pertaining to Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) implemented new counter terrorism designations. These measures aim to disrupt the financial networks and support structures of terrorist organizations globally.

The specific individuals and entities targeted in these designations have been identified as providing material, financial, or technological support to terrorist groups, or otherwise engaging in acts of terrorism.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Activities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This dual focus highlights the interconnectedness of various illicit networks.
These designations aim to sever financial ties and limit the operational capabilities of those contributing to the global drug trade and supporting terrorist organizations.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Information
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an update regarding existing Iran designations. This update provides additional information or modifications to previously announced sanctions.
Such updates are routinely issued to ensure the accuracy and effectiveness of sanctions programs, reflecting ongoing intelligence and enforcement efforts.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in Iran-related activities. These actions are part of the U.S. government's comprehensive strategy to pressure the Iranian regime.
The designations aim to disrupt networks supporting Iran's destabilizing activities and its proliferation of weapons.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes Cuba Sanctions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations targeting cyber-related malicious actors and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to combat illicit activities that pose a threat to U.S. national security and financial systems.

In a separate action, OFAC also imposed new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures target specific individuals and entities associated with the Cuban government and its economy, particularly those involved in crude oil shipping networks, state-owned entities, and China-based suppliers to Cuba's military forces.
The determination paves the way for potential sanctions on the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations, Issues Venezuela GL Amendment
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and provided updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to counter the Iranian regime's activities.

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert, warning maritime service providers of designation and penalty risks associated with vessels using false flags to evade Iran sanctions. The alert encourages enhanced due diligence where registration claims appear false.

In a separate development, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a related Frequently Asked Question were issued, providing updated guidance on authorized transactions involving the PDVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond, postponing the authorization until December 18, 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.
General Licenses are often updated to reflect evolving policy considerations or to provide further clarity on permissible activities under sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes North Korea and DRC-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities related to North Korea. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programs and other illicit activities.
Additionally, OFAC imposed designations related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These measures aim to address human rights abuses and corruption within the region.

articles.headline: EU Expands Sanctions Against Russia, Targeting 113 Individuals and Entities
body: The European Union has adopted new restrictive measures against Russia, adding 12 individuals and 101 entities to its sanctions lists. These actions are a response to Russia's continued aggression against Ukraine, particularly its intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure.

The new listings include nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, aiming to further cut off financial channels that fund Russia's war effort. The package also targets individuals and businesses in the Russian oil and energy sector, as well as those involved in e-commerce.

Separately, the Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2558 expanded the restrictive measures regime addressing Russia's destabilizing activities, adding 30 individuals and one entity to the sanctions list. These designations took effect upon publication in the Official Journal of the EU on November 16, 2026.

articles.headline: Fed Minutes Reveal Policymakers Leaning Towards Further Rate Hikes
body: Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October 27-28 meeting indicate that 'almost all' policymakers believe further interest rate hikes will likely be necessary to combat persistently high inflation. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) had voted 10-2 to hold rates steady at a target range of 3.75% to 4.00% at that meeting, citing the need for more data.

Two voting members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of an immediate 25-basis-point hike in October. Some officials are now considering a 50-basis-point increase at the upcoming December meeting, with Fed Governor Chris Waller expressing 'very, very concerned' about inflation.

The staff's economic outlook for 2026 is slightly stronger than previously forecast, driven by incoming data and AI-related investment. However, inflation is still expected to remain elevated, with the federal funds rate path implied by futures prices suggesting a high probability of a 25 basis point hike by year-end and two more by summer 2027.

articles.headline: Estonia Closes Russian Border Crossings, Citing Security Concerns
body: Estonia has formally decided to close all its road border crossings with Russia to the east and south for a preliminary six-month period, starting December 1. The Estonian government will decide next year whether to extend the closure.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stated that the border closure is an 'important measure' to reduce opportunities for exploiting cross-border movement to recruit individuals, conduct influence operations, organize acts of sabotage, or circumvent sanctions. This action follows Estonia's accusation that Russia was behind an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems, an accusation denied by the Kremlin.

Russia has condemned Estonia's decision, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova accusing Tallinn of planning to build a 'new Iron Curtain' and promising a response to safeguard Russia's national interests.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
